draft.why_angle: None of the rival pages quote Plex's own rule that hardware transcoding "is not currently possible inside of virtual machines". Several of them, and ChatGPT's answers, tell shoppers to pass the iGPU to a Docker VM, which is the layout Plex says won't work. This page uses Plex's and Proxmox's documentation to put Plex in a container on the host and keep the VMs off the GPU. It then compares all-in-one boxes by the RAM they ship with, since that decides whether two VMs fit under $800.
must: Plex says hardware transcoding is not possible inside virtual machines

page.title: Best all-in-one home server under $800 for Docker, Plex and a couple of VMs (2026)
page.h1: Best all-in-one home server under $800 for Docker, Plex and a couple of VMs (2026)
page.desc: Plex can't hardware-transcode inside a VM, so run it in Docker on an Intel Quick Sync host and spend the budget on RAM that comes fitted. Four-bay and mini PC picks priced 2026-11-13.
page.answer: Short answer. The best all-in-one home server under $800 for Docker, Plex and a couple of VMs is the TerraMaster F4-424 Pro: 32GB fitted, 4 bays, Intel Quick Sync. Run Plex in Docker or a Proxmox LXC on the host, not a VM: Plex says hardware transcoding is not possible inside virtual machines.

page.after:
What the differences mean

We earn nothing on the F4-424 Pro, and its link goes to TerraMaster's own store. It wins because it is the only Intel four-bay box here that ships with 32 GB under $800.

  • Getting to 32 GB. The F4-424 Pro ships with 32 GB for $759.99. TerraMaster sells a 32 GB DDR5 stick on its own for $699.99. The DXP4800 Plus plus the 32 GB DDR5 kit Bitdoze priced at $569.98 comes to $619.99 + $569.98 = $1,189.97.
  • Barebones. The WTR Max Intel at $529 plus that $569.98 kit comes to $1,098.98, before any SSD. The MS-01 SE costs $775 configured and $375 barebone, so Minisforum charges $775 − $375 = $400 for 32 GB plus 1 TB.
  • Memory for a couple of VMs. With 32 GB, two 8 GB VMs leave 32 − 16 = 16 GB for the NAS OS, Docker and Plex. With the DXP4800 Plus's 8 GB, one VM at the 4 GB Mighty Gadget used leaves 8 − 4 = 4 GB for everything else.

The DXP4800 Plus is the cheapest Intel four-bay here with 10GbE, and it comes with 8 GB. Mighty Gadget ran a Debian VM (2 vCPU, 4 GB) on it "acceptably", and Jellyfin transcoded 4K HEVC to 1080p in real time at about 20% CPU. That suits Plex and Docker with one light VM: {buy:ugreen-nasync-dxp4800-plus}

Where Plex goes when the same box runs VMs

Plex's support article on hardware-accelerated streaming (last modified 2026-10-27) says it "is not currently possible inside of virtual machines, as virtual machine hosts do not expose low-level video hardware to the guest operating system." The supported route is Docker. If the Docker host has an Intel Quick Sync CPU, you bind-mount the kernel device (/dev/dri) into the Plex container. It needs an active Plex Pass. Plex's Linux encoder list has Intel VAAPI, NVIDIA NVENC and software x264, with no AMD entry.

So run Plex and your other Docker apps in containers on the host with /dev/dri, and use the couple of VMs for things that need a whole OS, such as Home Assistant or a Windows test box, without a GPU. On Proxmox, give a Plex LXC the iGPU with the container's dev[n] passthrough option (pct manual, Proxmox VE 9.2.13). Don't pass the iGPU to a VM: Proxmox's PCI passthrough page warns that "if you pass through a device to a virtual machine, you cannot use that device anymore on the host."

On the NAS picks you don't need to set anything up. TerraMaster's TOS has Docker Manager with docker-compose and Portainer (NASCompares). TOS 7 adds a Virtual Machines module and lists the F4-424 Pro as compatible (NASCompares, Rob Andrews, 2025-12-15). NASCompares played media on the F4-424 Pro with hardware transcoding enabled, including some 8K.

Not recommended

Aoostar WTR Pro (Ryzen 7 5825U) for Plex. It is the cheapest box here with four bays, but it has Radeon graphics, and AMD is not on Plex's Linux encoder list, so Plex transcodes on the CPU. Consider it only if every player direct-plays.

Barebones plus retail DDR5. The WTR Max Intel has Quick Sync and six bays, but 32 GB of DDR5 takes it past $1,000 before an SSD. The MS-01 SE takes DDR4, not DDR5, so the cheap way to get it is Minisforum's 32 GB / 1 TB build at $775. The $375 barebone was out of stock on 2026-11-13.
